source.title: Finding Culture-Sensitive Neurons in Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Xiu-Tian Zhao; Rochelle Choenni; Rohit Saxena; Ivan Titov

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figures are represented only by captions or flattened visual content.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses neuron-level activation analysis and neuron deactivation as tools to investigate culture-sensitive processing in vision-language models. Its experiments do not test the claim versions’ stated shares of interpretable neurons, explanation quality, or attribution graphs.
record.gate_note: The study identifies neurons associated with culture subsets and tests their deactivation on held-out culturally grounded VQA. This is not a measurement of how many neuron poles have one or two understandable jobs, nor a test of explanations predicting held-out activations. Its culture-selectivity ablation results are recorded under fits_no_version. The cited work’s findings are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The study selects culture-sensitive decoder MLP neurons in three 7B VLMs by activation-frequency statistics and ablates them on CVQA. It never explains neurons, counts neuron poles with one or two jobs, scores explanations by simulation, builds attribution graphs, or analyses InceptionV1. Neuron-level selectivity is used as a tool, and the paper reports only its own selectors' ablation effects. It explicitly says it does not imply neurons are exclusively dedicated to culture.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that targeted ablations of decoder neurons selectively disrupt culture-specific VQA performance. ConAct gives the largest self-drops with minimal spillover on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Pangea-7B, while LLaVA-v1.6-Mistral-7B resists specific targeting. The identified neurons concentrate in model- and selector-dependent decoder layers.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses activation-frequency-based culture selectors and inference-time neuron deactivation, rather than neuron explanation scoring or the claimed audit of understandable neuron poles.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary by model and identification method. ConAct gives the largest self-deactivation accuracy drops for Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Pangea-7B; LLaVA-v1.6-Mistral-7B has weaker self–cross separation. Culture grouping also changes outcomes in the India and Spanish analyses.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating the top 1% of culture-selected decoder MLP neurons (ConAct/MAD) lowers self-culture accuracy by about 4–5.5 pp in Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Pangea-7B, with under 1.4 pp cross-culture change. Random 1% masks change accuracy by at most about 1 pp. LLaVA-v1.6-Mistral-7B shows weak self–cross separation (gap under 1 pp).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In some 7B VLMs, small sets of decoder neurons selected by culture-contrastive activation contribute relatively specifically to culture-tagged VQA. The specificity depends on model and selector, and the paper does not claim these neurons are monosemantic.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The evidence concerns English-translated CVQA questions and decoder MLP neurons only; it does not cover attention heads, vision encoders, or alignment modules. Selection uses fixed hyperparameters and activation-frequency summaries. No uncertainty estimates are stated. The measured culture categories are benchmark country–language groupings, which the authors caution do not capture the diversity within cultures.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 LAP and LAPE self/cross results and their self–cross gaps were not extracted; the retained Table 2 rows prioritize ConAct, MAD, and the random control. Appendix C’s individual India and Spanish cross-ablation values and the layer-count plots in Figures 5–7 were also left out; these are additional culture-grouping or layer-distribution analyses, not direct tests of the claim versions.

untested.parts: No share of neuron poles with one main job, two related jobs, or not understood; Qwen3-32B not studied.
No interpretable-neuron shares measured in any model. Only three 7B VLMs studied; no MoE or trillion-parameter models.
No InceptionV1, cat-and-car neuron, pose, or recursive generalization analysis.
No comparison of architecture, regularization or tools as causes of interpretability; no interpretable-share estimates.
No attribution graphs, replacement models or reconstruction error.
No explanations written from activating examples, and no test of whether they predict firing.

record.verdict_notes: Not a test of any version. The paper's framing of 'relative culture-selectivity, not exclusive dedication' is related to but distinct from the claim's one-main-job audit. Table 6 reports that 12.27% (Qwen) and 9.57% (Pangea) of neurons have cross-culture std above their mean. That is a variance statistic, not an interpretability share, and does not bear on V1/V2.

versions.untested_parts: Does not estimate the share of neuron poles with one or two main jobs or the share not understood.
Tests three 7B vision-language models, but does not measure the claimed shares, cover dense and mixture-of-experts language models, or test scaling up to trillions of parameters.
Does not analyze InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization versus superposition.
Does not compare architecture, regularization, or tool quality as causes of interpretability, or estimate interpretable-neuron shares in InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Does not build attribution graphs or compare neuron-based explanations with replacement models or reconstruction error.
Uses separate identification and evaluation splits for neuron selection and ablation, but does not test whether explanations written from activating examples predict where a neuron fires.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text or report the share of neurons with good explanation scores.
